sources.title: CVE-2021-45232: NVD vulnerability record
sources.snippet: In Apache APISIX Dashboard before 2.10.1, the Manager API uses two frameworks and introduces framework `droplet` on the basis of framework `gin`, all APIs and authentication middleware are developed based on framework `droplet`, but some API directly use the interface of framework `gin` thus bypassing the authentication.
supports: NVD lists CVE-2021-45232 as a research lead; product identity, version applicability, and exploitation remain unverified.

sources.title: Admin API - Apache APISIX
sources.snippet: UNTRUSTED WEB RESEARCH (not PCAP evidence). This article introduces the functions supported by the Apache APISIX Admin API, which you can use to get, create, update, and delete resources. | Webpage text: [PARTIAL WEBPAGE: only first 150000 bytes examined] 🤔 Introducing APISIX AI Gateway – Built for LLMs and AI workloads. Learn More The Admin API lets users control their deployed Apache APISIX instance. The architecture design gives an idea about how everything fits together. When APISIX is started, the Admin API will listen on port 9180 by default and take the API prefixed with /apisix/admin. Therefore, to avoid conflicts between your designed API and /apisix/admin, you can modify the configuration file /conf/config.yaml to modify the default listening port. APISIX supports setting the IP access allowlist of Admin API to prevent APISIX from being illegally accessed and attacked. You can configure the IP addresses to allow access in the deployment.admin.allow_admin option in the ./conf/config.yaml file. The X-API-KEY shown below refers to the deployment.admin.admin_key.key in the ./conf/config.yaml file, which is the access token for the Admin API. For security reasons, please modify the default admin_key, and check the allow_admin IP access list. key: your-admin-key # set a secure Admin API key; if left empty, APISIX will generate one during initialization and write it back to this file allow_admin: # http://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_access_module.html#allow ip: 0.0.0.0 # Specific IP, if not set, the default value is `0.0.0.0`. port: 9180 # Specific port, which must be different from node_listen's port. Using environment variables To configure via environment variables, you can use the ${{VAR}} syntax. For instance: And then run export ADMIN_KEY=$your_admin_key before running make init. If the configured environment variable can’t be found, an error will be thrown. If you want to use a default value when the environment variable is not set, use ${{VAR:=default_value}} instead. For instance: key: ${{ADMIN_KEY:=your-admin-key}} This will find the environment variable ADMIN_KEY first, and if it does not exist, it will use the fallback value you provided in the configuration. You can also specify environment variables in yaml keys. This is specifically useful in the standalone mode where you can specify the upstream nodes as follows: "${{HOST_IP}}:${{PORT}}": 1 By default, the Admin API checks for references between resources and will refuse to delete resources in use. You can make a force deletion by adding the request argument force=true to the delete request, for example: You can fetch the admin_key from config.yaml and save to an environment variable with the following command: admin_key=$(yq '.deployment.admin.admin_key[0].key' conf/config.yaml | sed 's/"//g') $ curl http://127.0.0.1:9180/apisix/admin/upstreams/1 -H "X-API-KEY: $admin_key" -X PUT -d '{ $ curl http://127.0.0.1:9180/apisix/admin/routes/1 -H "X-API-KEY: $admin_key" -X PUT -d '{ {"value":{"priority":0,"upstream_id":1,"uri":"/*","create_time":1689038794,"id":"1","status":1,"update_time":1689038916},"key":"/apisix/routes/1"} $ curl http://127.0.0.1:9180/apisix/admin/upstreams/1 -H "X-API-KEY: $admin_key" -X DELETE {"error_msg":"can not delete this upstream, route [1] is still using it now"} $ curl "http://127.0.0.1:9180/apisix/admin/upstreams/1?force=anyvalue" -H "X-API-KEY: $admin_key" -X DELETE {"error_msg":"can

sources.title: Configure Routes - Apache APISIX
sources.snippet: UNTRUSTED WEB RESEARCH (not PCAP evidence). This tutorial guides you through creating a Route using the APISIX Ingress Controller and verifying its behavior. | Webpage text: 🤔 Introducing APISIX AI Gateway – Built for LLMs and AI workloads. Learn More Apache APISIX provides flexible gateway management capabilities based on routes, in which routing paths and target upstreams are defined. This tutorial guides you through creating a Route using the APISIX Ingress Controller and verifying its behavior. You’ll configure a Route to a sample Upstream pointing to an httpbin service, then send a request to observe how APISIX proxies the traffic. Complete Get APISIX and APISIX Ingress Controller. Install the httpbin example application on the cluster to test the configuration: kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apache/apisix-ingress-controller/refs/heads/v2.1.0/examples/httpbin/deployment.yaml In this section, you will create a Route that forwards client requests to the httpbin example application, an HTTP request and response service. You can use either Gateway API, Ingress, or APISIX CRD resources to configure the route. If you are using Gateway API, you should first configure the GatewayClass and Gateway resources: Show configurationapiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 namespace: ingress-apisix controllerName: apisix.apache.org/apisix-ingress-controller apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 namespace: ingress-apisix The port in the Gateway listener can be used for route matching based on listener_port_match_mode (off by default; auto or explicit opt in). The controller cannot dynamically open new ports on the data plane, so ensure APISIX is configured to listen on the port. If you are using Ingress or APISIX custom resources, you can proceed without additional configuration, as the IngressClass resource below is already applied with installation: Show configurationapiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 controller: apisix.apache.org/apisix-ingress-controller apiGroup: apisix.apache.org namespace: ingress-apisix See Define Controller and Gateway for more information on parameters. Create a Kubernetes manifest file for a Route that proxy requests to httpbin: apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 namespace: ingress-apisix apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 namespace: ingress-apisix apiVersion: apisix.apache.org/v2 namespace: ingress-apisix - name: getting-started-ip Apply the configurations to your cluster: kubectl apply -f httpbin-route.yaml Expose the service port to your local machine by port forwarding: kubectl port-forward svc/apisix-gateway 9080:80 & Send a request to the Route: curl "http://127.0.0.1:9080/ip" You should see a response similar to the following: Edit this page on GitHub Report an issue
